Beta. Served in production; the API can still change.

Schemas and Codegen ​

A database's models are declared once, in a type: a TOML file in your config tree. That one file is the schema for everything that touches the data:

  • Your web and iOS apps generate typed model classes from it.
  • Your server functions get a typed handle from it: ctx.db3(id, "<type>").model("<model>") only accepts models the type declares.
  • The database itself enforces it: a typed database refuses records of models the type doesn't declare, and runs the type's rules on every write.

Many databases share one type — every team's workspace, every class's gradebook — so a change to the type reaches all of them at once.

Declaring a type ​

Scaffold one with primitive config create db3-type <name>, or write the file yourself under primitive/<env>/db3-types/:

toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/workspace.toml
[type]
name = "workspace"
timestamps = { create = "createdAt", update = "updatedAt" }

[models.tasks]
class_name = "Task"

[models.tasks.fields.title]
type = "string"
required = true

[models.tasks.fields.completed]
type = "boolean"
default = false

[models.tasks.fields.priority]
type = "number"
indexed = true

[models.tasks.fields.status]
type = "string"
enum = ["open", "doing", "done"]
default = "open"

[models.tasks.fields.tags]
type = "stringset"
max_count = 10

[models.tasks.fields.createdAt]
type = "number"

[models.tasks.fields.updatedAt]
type = "number"

[models.members]
class_name = "Member"

[models.members.fields.email]
type = "string"
unique = true

primitive config push sends it. The model key (tasks) is the name records are stored under and what server functions and the CLI use; class_name is the generated class or struct (Task). swift-bao-codegen refuses a model whose Swift name is TypedQueryModel, PrimitiveModel or PrimitiveRowDecodable; set class_name to another name. A model needs no id field: every record has one, minted on create. primitive config fields db3-type lists a type file's top-level keys.

Pushing and deleting types is for app admins and owners, and a type takes no rule set. primitive config push refuses a type file with a ruleSetName or ruleSetId line, and PUT db3-types/{name} refuses a ruleSetId with DB3_TYPE_RULE_SET_UNSUPPORTED. Delete the line, or run primitive config pull, which rewrites the file without it.

Models shared by several types ​

When two types hold the same model — a securities catalog in a reference database and in every household's database — declare it once and name it from the other type with [type] models:

toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/household.toml
[type]
name = "household"
models = ["securities"]   # declared in reference.toml

[models.accounts.fields.name]
type = "string"

models names models declared under [models.<key>] in another file of the same db3-types/ directory. primitive config push sends each type with the named declarations included, so a field added to securities reaches both types. Once any type names a shared model, the db3-types/ files hold one shape per model: push refuses a name no file declares and two files that declare one model differently, naming the files and the fields.

Fields ​

TypeHolds
stringText. enum types the generated field as one of the listed values; add enforce_enum = true to refuse any write outside them (see Enforcing an enum).
numberA number. Integers are exact up to ±2^53.
booleantrue or false.
dateAn ISO 8601 date or date-time string (a number is also accepted).
idA record id. Every record has an id, minted on create; declare the field only to set its options.
stringsetA set of strings: each value once, members changed individually. max_count caps the members and max_length each member's length, checked by the clients.
vectorA fixed-length list of numbers, such as an embedding. dims is how many; element is how each is stored: f32, f16 or i8. See Vector fields.

Each field also takes required, default, indexed (index it for fast equality queries — each index adds to every write, so index only fields you query; you can add one later), unique (no two records share the value), auto_assign (generate a value on create) and auto_stamp (create, update or both: stamp the write time, in epoch milliseconds, whichever side writes).

A default is written when a record is created without the field. A string, number, boolean, date or id field with a literal default also reads as the default whenever a record lacks the field, holds it as null, or holds a value of another kind ("5" in a number field, 1 in a boolean field): task.completed is false for a record created before you declared the default.

Every read does this: the generated web and iOS models, a function's ctx.db3 and the record routes. So each types the field non-optional (completed: boolean on the web and in a function's Db3 row, completed: Bool on iOS), and a create may still leave it out. A database fills from the revision of its type that it holds. In a document with Yjs state, a stored 0 or 1 in a boolean field reads false or true.

The read stores nothing: a field saved as null stays null, and a database change trigger receives the stored row. A read that selects fields, such as an include's projection, fills only the fields it selects. A string set's default, a generator such as "$now" and a field the database's type clears are never filled, and keep their optional types.

A unique key over several fields is a named constraint:

toml
[[models.categories.unique_constraints]]
name = "name_parentId"
fields = ["name", "parentId"]

A unique constraint applies to scalar fields only. A type that marks a stringset unique is refused with UNIQUE_ON_STRINGSET, and a client model that declares one throws UniqueStringsetError.

Gotchas

  • Filters, sorts and counts compare stored values, so { completed: false } does not match a record stored without completed, though it reads false. Add { completed: { $exists: false } } under $or to match both.
  • An include relates records by stored values. A record stored without its sourceField relates to no record, even when the field reads a default id.

Enforcing an enum ​

By default enum only types the generated field. Add enforce_enum = true and the database refuses any write that would leave a value outside the set, from every writer: an app, a function, the CLI and a bulk load.

toml
[models.tasks.fields.status]
type = "string"
enum = ["open", "doing", "done"]
enforce_enum = true
default = "open"

A write of "archived" to status is refused with DB3_VALUE_NOT_IN_ENUM, and the message names the record, the field, the values and what was written. An app's device refuses it before anything is sent. null, a write that leaves the field out, and a delete are not checked.

enforce_enum takes true or false; any other value is refused when the type is read. It belongs to a string field with an enum (written out or through a shared enum ref), never to the id field, and an enforced field's default must be one of the values. Only a type used by db3s can carry it: a database type with databases of it is refused with ENFORCE_ENUM_DB3_ONLY.

Turning enforcement on, or removing a value from an enforced enum, is checked against each database's records. A database whose live records hold a value outside the set is refused with DB3_TYPE_REFUSED: the reason names the field, how many records hold such a value, and up to three of them as [id, value]. That database keeps the revision it had and its writes stay unchecked; fix those records and push again (or retry the push). The other databases of the type take the new revision.

Gotchas

  • An app on an older client library receives the refusal as DOCUMENT_ENTRY_INVALID, after the write was sent. Update the client to have its device refuse first and to branch on DB3_VALUE_NOT_IN_ENUM.

Shared enums ​

When several fields take the same set of values, declare the set once in a schemas/ file and give each field a ref to it:

toml
# primitive/dev/schemas/common.toml
[defs.Status]
type = "string"
enum = ["open", "doing", "done"]
toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/workspace.toml
[type]
name = "workspace"

[models.tasks.fields.status]
ref = "Status"
indexed = true
default = "open"

primitive config push sends the field as type = "string" with the def's values, so the stored type, the generated models and ctx.db3 all see enum = ["open", "doing", "done"]. Edit the def and push again to change every field that refs it; config diff shows each such type as modified until you do. config pull keeps a field's ref while the def still gives the values the server holds.

A ref names the def in one of three forms: "Status" when exactly one schemas/ file declares it, "common.Status" (the file and the def), or "schemas.common.Status". Push refuses "common.Status" when common is also the key of a function, prompt or db3 type, and lists the long forms to choose from. A shared enum def is a plain string enum: type = "string", a non-empty enum of distinct strings, and optionally description, title, examples, deprecated and $comment. Beside ref, write the field's other options, but not type or enum.

Codegen reads the schemas/ directory beside the db3-types/ it is given. On the web, each shared enum is one type: js-bao-codegen-v2 writes shared-enums.generated.ts beside the models, exporting Status and StatusValues (the values in the def's order), types each field that refs the def as Status, and re-exports both from the generated index.ts:

ts
import { Task, StatusValues, type Status } from "./models";

function advance(task: Task, next: Status = StatusValues[1]) {
  task.status = next; // "archived" does not compile
}

The function helpers in functions/generated/ declare the same Status, so values pass between a model and a function with no conversion. A def named like something a generated file already declares or imports (a model class, BaseModel, JsBaoClient) is exported, or imported, as Schemas_<File>_<Name>, for example Schemas_Common_Status.

On iOS, the type is the enum Status that primitive functions codegen --lang swift declares in Primitive.generated.swift; the template's scripts/codegen.sh writes it whenever the environment has schemas/ files. A struct field that refs the def is a Status?, and its stored text is statusRaw, so a value another client wrote outside the enum reads as nil and is kept:

swift
var task = Task(title: "Ship", status: .open)
task.status = .done // a String does not compile
if task.status == nil, let raw = task.statusRaw { print("unknown status \(raw)") }

The Swift function helpers type their inputs and outputs with the same Status, so a function's result passes to a model with no conversion.

For each type file that uses a ref, js-bao-codegen-v2 also writes <file>.toml.generated.ts, holding the type with its refs expanded, and the generated index.ts registers that in place of the type file, whatever --schema-import names.

Gotchas

  • Codegen checks a "<file>.<Name>" ref against the schemas/ and db3-types/ keys only. Write the long form when a function or prompt shares the file's key, or push refuses what codegen accepted.
  • The SwiftPM codegen plugin runs again when a type file changes. After editing only a def in schemas/, clean the build folder so the generated structs pick up the new values.
  • Load a type that uses ref on iOS through its generated models; TomlSchemaLoader reads fields as written.
  • On iOS a field that refs a shared enum is a Status?, not a String?. Compare it with a case (.open) or read statusRaw, and pass a case to the initializers. statusEnum and Task.StatusValue are deprecated, and Task.StatusValue is not generated when a shared enum the model refs is itself named StatusValue. The app target must compile Primitive.generated.swift, or the build stops with "cannot find type 'Status'".

Vector fields ​

A vector field holds a fixed number of numbers — an embedding from a model, say:

toml
[models.notes.fields.embedding]
type = "vector"
dims = 768
element = "f16"

Your app writes and reads numbers; the record stores their bytes as base64 text. element trades precision for size:

elementEach number768 numbers take
f32A 32-bit float, exact for what a Float32Array or [Float] holds3,072 bytes (4,096 base64 characters)
f16A 16-bit float, rounded to nearest; magnitudes up to 655041,536 bytes (2,048 characters)
i8One signed byte, scaled to the vector's largest magnitude: within 1/254 of it772 bytes (1,032 characters)

A vector field takes required and no other option: no indexed, unique, default, enum, auto_assign, auto_stamp, max_length or max_count, and no unique constraint names one.

A write whose value doesn't fit the field — the wrong number of numbers, a number that isn't finite, an f16 value past 65504, or stored text that isn't the encoding's base64 — is refused with DB3_VECTOR_INVALID. A field's encoding is fixed once records hold values for it: a push that changes its dims or element, or declares an existing field as vector, is refused for such a database with DB3_TYPE_REFUSED. So type the database before you load embeddings into it; base64 text loaded into an untyped database can't become a vector field until those values are cleared.

JSON fields ​

When a field holds a structured value, such as an address, a list of tags or a map of weights, declare its shape as a def in a schemas/ file and give the field a ref to it. An object def (type = "object") types an object; a list def (type = "array") types a list of its items; an object def whose additionalProperties is a schema types a map, each value of that schema whatever its key:

toml
# primitive/dev/schemas/addresses.toml
[defs.Address]
type = "object"
[defs.Address.fields.city]
type = "string"
required = true
[defs.Address.fields.zip]
type = "string"

[defs.Tags]
type = "array"
items = { type = "string" }
maxItems = 10

[defs.Weights]
type = "object"
additionalProperties = { type = "number", minimum = 0 }
toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/shop.toml
[type]
name = "shop"

[models.orders.fields.shipping_address]
ref = "Address"
required = true

[models.orders.fields.tags]
ref = "Tags"

[models.orders.fields.weights]
ref = "Weights"

The record stores the value as canonical JSON text (RFC 8785: keys sorted, no whitespace) in a plain string field: an object for an object def, and the array itself (["gift","fragile"]) for a list def. primitive config push sends the field as type = "string", and the stored type and db3 schema --toml show it that way. The ref takes the same three forms as a shared enum's, and beside it only required is allowed. No indexed, unique, default or other option, and no unique constraint can name the field.

In a function, ctx.db3 types the field Db3Json<Schemas.Address> (tags as Db3Json<Schemas.Tags>, a string[], and weights as Db3Json<Schemas.Weights>, a Record<string, number>). A plain string doesn't compile there, so convert with encodeDb3Json and decodeDb3Json from primitive-functions, which take an object or an array:

ts
import { encodeDb3Json, decodeDb3Json } from "primitive-functions";

const orders = ctx.db3(db3Id, "shop").model("orders");
const saved = await orders.save({ data: { shipping_address: encodeDb3Json({ city: "Lisbon" }) } });
const row = await orders.get(saved.record.id);
const address = row ? decodeDb3Json(row.shipping_address) : null; // Schemas.Address

On the web, the generated models read and write the field as an Address, tags as a string[] and weights as a Record<string, number>. The template's pnpm codegen needs no edit: whenever the environment has schemas/ files beside its types, it runs primitive functions codegen first and passes the defs module to the model generator. Outside the template, generate the defs module, then name it when you generate the models:

bash
primitive functions codegen -o src/types/generated/functions
npx js-bao-codegen-v2 -i ../primitive/dev/db3-types -o src/models \
  --schema-defs-import ../types/generated/functions/schema-defs.generated

primitive functions codegen writes schema-defs.generated.ts beside the function helpers (or into -o) whenever a db3 field refs an object or list def, declaring each such def's type and its compiled schema. --schema-defs-import is the module specifier the generated models import it by, written as given; js-bao-codegen-v2 refuses a type with a JSON field without it. Then:

ts
const order = new Order({ title: "First", shipping_address: { city: "Lisbon" } });
await order.save({ db3: db3Id });

order.shipping_address?.city; // "Lisbon"
order.shipping_address = { city: "Porto", zip: "4000" };
order.tags = ["gift", "fragile"];
order.weights = { box: 1.5, card: 0.1 };

A value that doesn't match the def is refused with Db3JsonValueError when you assign it, pass it to the constructor or to upsertByUnique, and nothing changes. Its path names where inside the value the problem is (value.city, value[1]), and reason says what it is. A read is frozen, so change the value by assigning a new object or array. Assigning null clears the field.

On iOS, primitive functions codegen --lang swift declares each such def's type in Primitive.generated.swift, with the alias Db3JSON_<file>_<Name> that the generated models use; the template's scripts/codegen.sh writes it whenever the environment has schemas/ files. The struct's field is a Db3JSON_addresses_Address?, an Address; tags is a [String] and weights a [String: Double]:

swift
var order = Order(title: "First", shipping_address: Address(city: "Lisbon"))
order = try order.save(in: db3Id)

order.shipping_address?.city // "Lisbon"
order.shipping_address?.zip = "1000"
order = try order.save(in: db3Id)

A save whose value doesn't match the def throws Db3JSONValueError, with the same path and reason, and writes nothing. Assigning nil clears the field.

A query can only ask whether the field holds a value: { shipping_address: { $exists: true } }. Equality compares the stored text, so don't use it to compare values. You can't filter on a path inside the value, sort by it or index it.

A JSON field's def may use these keywords: type, enum, properties (or fields), required, additionalProperties (a boolean, or a schema each undeclared key's value must match), a single-schema items, oneOf, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern, minItems, maxItems, and the annotations (title, description, default, format, examples, $comment, deprecated, readOnly, writeOnly). Push and primitive functions codegen refuse any other keyword, naming the def, the field and the keyword.

Gotchas

  • Only the generated web and iOS models check a value against the def. A function's write isn't checked, and neither are bulk loads, raw client.db3 record writes or another app's older client: the server stores any string. Validate in the function when the value comes from outside.
  • Stored text whose root isn't the def's kind (an object, or an array for a list def) reads as undefined on the web, with one console warning per field, so the generated getter's type includes undefined, and null (an unchecked write can clear the field), even for a required field, and db3JsonText(order, "shipping_address") from js-bao returns the text. On iOS, text that doesn't decode into the field's type reads as nil and stays in shipping_addressRaw. On both, saving the record's other fields leaves it as it is. Reads aren't checked against the def, so rows written before the def changed still read on the web.
  • A number above 2^53 in magnitude (1e21 included) is refused: encodeDb3Json throws DB3_JSON_INVALID, and an iOS save throws Db3JSONValueError, an Int included. Store such a number as a string.
  • minLength and maxLength count Unicode code points, so an emoji counts as one character, and a flag, two.
  • A pattern must use syntax that both JavaScript and NSRegularExpression accept, and no backreference (\1, \k<name>): the two evaluate them differently, so push and primitive functions codegen refuse one.
  • To change a def without stranding stored rows, add optional fields rather than renaming or requiring them. An iOS app built against the older def drops the fields its struct doesn't declare when it saves the value.
  • The iOS app target must compile Primitive.generated.swift, or the build stops with "cannot find type 'Db3JSON_addresses_Address'".
  • An app build older than this release reads a list field as undefined on the web and nil on iOS. Ship the updated app before relying on list values that its installed builds read.
  • To convert an existing string field, replace its type = "string" with the ref. Its stored values must already be JSON of the def's kind: objects for an object def, arrays for a list def.
  • A JSON field belongs to a type in db3-types/ with a [type] table. A ref to an object or list def anywhere else is refused.
  • A function or prompt schema can't ref a map def (one whose additionalProperties is a schema): push and primitive functions codegen refuse it with additionalProperties must be true or false. Keep map defs for JSON fields.

Relationships ​

Declare how models point at each other, and the generated models gain typed accessors and include builders:

toml
# A post refers to its author; an author has many posts.
[models.posts.relationships.author]
type = "refersTo"
model = "authors"
related_id_field = "authorId"

[models.authors.relationships.posts]
type = "hasMany"
model = "posts"
related_id_field = "authorId"
order_by_field = "createdAt"
order_direction = "DESC"

# Many-to-many through a join model.
[models.posts.relationships.tags]
type = "hasManyThrough"
model = "tags"
join_model = "postTags"
join_model_local_field = "postId"
join_model_related_field = "tagId"

Related records load in the same query with include — see Loading related records.

Generating code ​

Point every codegen at the same type files, so the web app, the iOS app and your functions always agree on the models. Give codegen the db3-types/ directory: it reads every type file in it and generates each model once, so an app whose clients open several kinds of database gets one set of models and one registration list.

Web. The template's pnpm codegen script needs no edit: dev, build and test run it first, and it runs js-bao's code generator once per type file in the environment's db3-types/. Each type gets its own src/models/<type>/, and src/models/index.ts exports an allModels holding every type's classes, which you pass to the client at startup. A model shared through [type] models is generated only in the folder of the type that declares it.

To generate only the types the web client opens, name them in a bao-codegen.json beside its package.json:

json
{ "types": ["notes", "contacts"] }

Each entry is a type file's name without .toml, looked up in the environment codegen generates for, so one file serves every environment. With no file, every type is generated. A type left out loses its src/models/<type>/ on the next run.

Watch out when selecting types:

  • Select the type that declares a model another selected type names in [type] models, or that model gets no class.
  • Every selected type must exist in each environment the app builds or deploys for. Codegen stops on a name with no type file, before it writes anything.
  • The template generates with known types only, so the client refuses to create or open a database of a type left out.

Outside the template, run the generator directly over the whole directory:

bash
npx js-bao-codegen-v2 -i ../primitive/dev/db3-types -o src/models

-i also takes one type file, or several (-i household.toml -i reference.toml). The generator writes one <Class>.generated.ts per model across every input, and one index.ts exporting allModels. Each generated file's header names the type files it came from. --schema-import names the barrel's single schema import, so it is refused when more than one input declares models; the template's script passes it on each one-file run. A type with a JSON field also needs --schema-defs-import, which the template's script passes for you.

iOS. The template's scripts/codegen.sh regenerates the model structs on every scripted build path (./build.sh, ./run.sh, ./test.sh) and every Xcode build; a bare swift build compiles the committed output. It reads the type files named in a bao-codegen.json at the root of the app target's sources; paths resolve against that directory. Name the type directory to generate every kind of database the app opens:

json
{ "inputs": ["../../primitive/dev/db3-types"] }

inputs also takes type files, and several entries; every named type is generated into Models/Generated/ with one GeneratedModels barrel. One type file can be named on its own as { "input": "../../primitive/dev/db3-types/workspace.toml" }. The same file drives the SwiftPM codegen plugin in a package that runs it itself.

On any other build path, run the generator directly: swift run swift-bao-codegen --input primitive/dev/db3-types --output Sources/<App>/Models/Generated from the package root. --input takes a type file or a directory, and can be repeated. Register the generated models once at startup with GeneratedModels.register(on: client).

Server functions. primitive config push (and primitive functions codegen) types the Db3 namespace of functions/primitive.d.ts from every type in the tree. With it, ctx.db3(id, "workspace") accepts only a type that exists, .model("tasks") only a model that type declares, and rows come back typed. A type's timestamps fields are required numbers on the rows a read returns from the models it stamps; writes leave them out.

More than one client in one process. A generated model class binds to the first client that uses it. A Node script, worker or test harness that creates a second client in the same process shares that binding, so the second client's model calls — reads, writes and subscriptions alike — route to the first client instead of its own. A save through such a class into a database only the second client holds is refused with DB3_MODEL_ON_OTHER_CLIENT, and nothing is written. Give each client its own model classes, or read and write through client.db3.records(id) instead of the generated models; it offers the same operations and needs no bound class.

Adding a model to a running client. client.registerModel(Model) adds a model class after the client started, and the model works in every database the client already holds. The call waits for databases that are still connecting, for up to the client's registerModelTimeoutMs option (30 seconds by default). If one has not finished after a sixth of that (5 seconds by default, 10 at most), the client logs a warning naming it. When the bound passes, the call rejects with REGISTER_MODEL_TIMEOUT, and error.details.documentIds lists the databases it waited on. The model is not registered then; call registerModel again once they finish connecting. Raise the bound when a database legitimately takes longer to connect, such as a large one on a slow link:

ts
const client = await initializeClient({ ...options, registerModelTimeoutMs: 120_000 });

The client refuses a registerModelTimeoutMs that is not a positive number when it is built, with INVALID_ARGUMENT.

Known types ​

Generate an app's models with --known-types-only and its client refuses to create or open a database of any type it was not generated with. Without it, a typo or a database of another app's type gets created or opened as if it were untyped, and its records skip the models the app expects. The web template's pnpm codegen turns it on (a knownTypesOnly constant at the top of scripts/codegen.mjs). Elsewhere, pass the flag to either generator:

bash
npx js-bao-codegen-v2 -i ../primitive/dev/db3-types -o src/models --known-types-only
swift run swift-bao-codegen --input primitive/dev/db3-types --output Sources/<App>/Models/Generated --known-types-only

In a Swift package that runs the SwiftPM codegen plugin, say "knownTypesOnly": true in the target's bao-codegen.json, beside the input or inputs that names the types, and the plugin passes the flag:

json
{ "inputs": ["../../primitive/dev/db3-types"], "knownTypesOnly": true }

The iOS template's scripts/codegen.sh does not read this key yet and refuses a bao-codegen.json that has it.

The generated barrel declares every type in its input, archived ones marked. On iOS, GeneratedModels.register(on: client) registers them; call it at startup even when no model was generated. If start-up already loaded a stored copy of an unknown type from the device, the call refuses it: it stops answering queries, as below. With the setting on:

  • client.db3.create with a type the app was not generated with, or one archived in its type file, is refused on the device with INVALID_ARGUMENT before anything is created. The error's details.reason is "unknown-type", details.type names the type, details.knownTypes lists the types it may create, and details.archived is true for an archived one. getOrCreateWithAlias refuses an unknown type the same way and sends an archived one, so an alias that already names a database still answers it.
  • Subscribing to a database of an unknown type rejects ready and available with DB3_TYPE_UNKNOWN_TO_CLIENT (details.db3Id, details.type). Nothing of it is applied, the client does not retry it, and client.db3.state(id) carries the error. A client.db3.records(id) call on it is refused the same way before its request.
  • client.db3.stored() lists a copy of such a database with knownType: false and its type, and listMine() marks its rows knownType: false. Evict the copy with client.db3.evict(id) as any other.

allowUnknownType: true on create, getOrCreateWithAlias, subscribe (or refresh) and client.db3.records(id, …) lets one database through on that client. A database created or opened that way opens on the client for as long as it runs, and listings still mark it knownType: false:

ts
const subscription = client.db3.subscribe(db3Id);
try {
  await subscription.ready;
  return subscription;
} catch (error) {
  if ((error as { code?: string }).code !== "DB3_TYPE_UNKNOWN_TO_CLIENT") throw error;
  const escaped = client.db3.subscribe(db3Id, { allowUnknownType: true });
  await escaped.ready;
  return escaped;
}
swift
let subscription = try client.db3.subscribe(db3Id)
do {
  try await subscription.ready()
  return subscription
} catch let error as JsBaoError where error.code == .db3TypeUnknownToClient {
  var options = Db3SubscribeOptions()
  options.allowUnknownType = true
  let escaped = try client.db3.subscribe(db3Id, options: options)
  try await escaped.ready()
  return escaped
}

In TypeScript, the generated barrel also lists the app's types for client.db3.create({ type }), so an editor completes them; a computed string still compiles.

Gotchas

  • A type attached to a database a device already has open is refused at that device's next open of it: a reconnect, a new subscribe or a restart. Until then the open session stays live, and the server judges its writes by the type.
  • The guard is on the device only. Server functions, the CLI and the console create and open every type.

Typing a database ​

A database created with a type is typed from its first write:

bash
primitive db3 create "Q3 launch" --type workspace

In code, pass type to client.db3.create or getOrCreateWithAlias. A database created without one accepts records of any model; give it a type later with primitive db3 type attach <db3-id> workspace (or client.db3.setType). The attach is refused with DB3_TYPE_REFUSED, listing the reasons, when existing records break the type. A database's type never changes once set.

A database without a type takes its indexes and unique constraints from the model declarations of the clients that write it. A client declares to such a database only the models it uses there:

  • the models whose records the device's copy holds;
  • a model it writes there for the first time, declared just before that write, so a unique constraint holds from the first record;
  • the models bound to that database: a model whose default database it is (BaseModel.setModelDefaultDb3(model, id); Swift: client.setModelDefaultDb3(model, id)), and, when it is the client's default database (BaseModel.setDefaultDb3(id); Swift: client.setDefaultDb3(id)), every model without a default database of its own.

A model the app uses only in other databases, registered at startup or later (client.registerModel; Swift: client.registerModels), is not declared there. To put a model's indexes and unique constraints in force before any record of it exists, bind it to the database with setModelDefaultDb3 before you subscribe.

On a typed database:

  • A save of a model the type doesn't declare is refused with DB3_MODEL_NOT_DECLARED.
  • The type's indexes, unique constraints and rules apply to every writer — devices, functions and the CLI alike.
  • A client's own model declaration is not installed; the type is the declaration.

Changing a type ​

Edit the type's file and push it with primitive config push. The push reaches every database of the type in the background; follow it with primitive db3-types push-status workspace, and see what's pushed with primitive db3-types list and primitive db3-types get workspace.

What to write depends on what you want:

You want toWriteStored records and shipped builds
Add a model, a field or an enum value; make a field optional; edit indexed, unique, default or descriptionThe new declarationRecords without a new field read it as unset, or as its literal default; a field newly indexed or unique is indexed on every database of the type
Stop using a fielddeprecated = true, then cleared = true, then the name in removedFields (Retiring a field)Reads leave a cleared field out; its stored values are dropped as records are next written or read
Rename a fieldThe new key, with storedAs naming the old one (Renaming a field)Nothing is rewritten; shipped builds keep using the old name
Change a field's typeA new field, a function that copies the values, then retire the old field (Changing the type of a field)The old values stay readable until the old field is cleared
Remove a field or a model outrightallowFieldRemoval for the app, then --allow-field-removal (Removing fields on purpose)Only the declaration goes: stored values stay in records, server reads still return them, and builds that declare the field keep reading them. To hide the values, retire the field instead

Once a database of the type exists, a push can't make the records it stores unreadable. config push refuses these changes with DB3_TYPE_NOT_APPEND_ONLY, lists each one with its reason, and writes no type:

Refused changeDo instead
Removing a fieldRetire it
Removing a modelLeave it declared and stop writing it, or remove it on purpose
Changing a field's typeAdd a field of the new type and copy the values
Removing a value from a field's enumKeep the value, and stop writing it in app code
Making a field required, or adding a required field to an existing modelAdd the field without required, with a default if records need a value
Changing a vector field's dims or elementAdd a vector field of the new shape and embed into it

While no database of the type exists, every change pushes.

A database whose records break a revision the push allows — a new unique over existing duplicates, say — refuses it and keeps its previous revision whole; push-status names it, and primitive db3-types push <type> --retry <run-id> tries again once the records are fixed. Removing a type's file is refused by config push --prune with DB3_TYPE_IN_USE while any database is of that type.

Retiring a field ​

Retire a field in three pushes: deprecate it, clear it, then remove its name for good.

1. Deprecate. The field is still read and written; generated code marks it deprecated (@deprecated in TypeScript, @available(*, deprecated) in Swift), and config push lists each deprecated field still present.

toml
[models.tasks.fields.oldScore]
type = "number"
deprecated = true

2. Clear. Every read leaves the field out and every filter, sort and aggregate reads it as unset, on the server and on each device once it has the new revision. Writes that still send it are accepted and store nothing for it, and a record's stored value is dropped the next time the record is written or read. The field's index and single-field unique constraint go with it, and generated models lose it.

toml
[models.tasks.fields.oldScore]
type = "number"
deprecated = true
cleared = true

3. Remove. Move the cleared field's name into the model's removedFields. The name is reserved in that model for good: no type of the app that declares the model can declare it again, and it can't be taken out of removedFields. Deleting the last type that declares the model, once no database is of it, releases the name.

toml
[models.tasks]
removedFields = ["oldScore"]

Clearing is refused while a compound unique constraint, a trigger, autoPopulatedFields or timestamps names the field; remove that first. Un-clear a field by deleting cleared = true and pushing: every server read returns each value not yet dropped, and config push warns that the return is partial. primitive db3-types get <type> lists the type's deprecated, cleared and removed fields.

Gotchas

  • Clearing is not erasure. A record's value is dropped only when the record is next written or read, and earlier exports and the database's history keep it.
  • Make a required field optional first. Clearing a field stored as required is refused on a type with databases: push it without required, ship builds generated from that, then clear it. A build generated while the field was required stops reading records without it.
  • Remove a field's default first. Clearing a field stored with a literal default is refused on a type with databases (cleared-field-defaulted), even when the same push drops the default: push it without its default, ship builds generated from that, then clear it. An iOS build generated while the field had a default stops reading records of a database that holds the clear.
  • Drop indexes registered on a database first. A database with an index over several fields, a text index over several fields, or a vector index that names the field keeps the old revision; drop the index (DELETE /indexes/<name>), then primitive db3-types push <type> --retry <run-id>.
  • Un-clearing is partial. Values already dropped stay unset, and indexes registered on a database that the clear dropped are not restored. A device keeps its local copy, with what it held, until it next downloads the database whole.

Renaming a field ​

Rename a field by changing its key and naming the old name in storedAs. Records, indexes and builds generated before the rename keep the stored name; nothing is rewritten or reindexed.

Before:

toml
[models.tasks.fields.due]
type = "date"

After:

toml
[models.tasks.fields.dueDate]
type = "date"
storedAs = "due"

Push it as any other change, then regenerate your models from the renamed file. App code uses the new name; builds already shipped keep reading and writing the field as before:

ts
const task = new Task({ title: "Plan", dueDate: "2026-07-01" });
await task.save({ db3: db3Id });
const soon = await Task.query({ dueDate: { $lt: "2026-07-08" } }, { db3: db3Id, sort: { dueDate: 1 } });
swift
try Task(title: "Plan", dueDate: "2026-07-01").save(in: db3Id)
let f = Task.fields
let soon = try Task.query(where: f.dueDate.lt("2026-07-08"), sort: [.asc(f.dueDate)], options: QueryOptions(db3: [db3Id]))

A generated model writes the stored name for you, so its records, indexes and unique constraints are the same as before the rename. A single-field unique constraint keeps its name (tasks_due_unique). The push answer lists each rename in renamedFields, and primitive db3-types get workspace shows each field's former names. To rename it again, change the key and keep storedAs = "due"; a field can also take back one of its earlier names.

On the server a renamed field answers to every name it has had: record data, filters, sorts, aggregates, write conditions, index registrations, triggers, autoPopulatedFields and timestamps take dueDate, due or any former name. HTTP record routes answer the stored name (due) unless the request passes names=current:

bash
curl "$API/app/$APP_ID/api/db3/$DB3_ID/records/tasks?names=current" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# {"items":[{"id":"01J…","title":"Plan","dueDate":"2026-07-01"}], …}

Functions (ctx.db3) and the CLI's record commands answer current names.

client.db3.records(id) answers with your build's names. On a database whose type your build's models were generated from, it sends dueDate as due and answers dueDate, so a later rename never changes what a shipped build answers. On a database of any other type, on an untyped database, and for a model your build doesn't declare, it sends and answers stored names. In JavaScript the calls go to the server, which also accepts any former name; in Swift they read and write the device's copy, which takes the current and the stored name.

primitive db3 export writes a renamed field under its current name (dueDate), in its records and in its declaration, which keeps storedAs = "due". primitive db3 import loads it back under the stored name. An export taken before or after a rename imports into a database of the renamed type with this release of the CLI or later: it compares the export with the type by stored name.

Gotchas

  • A stored name never changes. Changing or removing an existing field's storedAs is refused like removing the field. Under the same key it is refused even with the override, because the key stays reserved to the old stored name. Keep storedAs on every later rename.
  • A name stays reserved in its model. A field can't take another field's current, stored or former name, or a removed field's. storedAs can't be id.
  • Name each field a hook reads. A trigger or auto-populated expression that uses record whole, or reads a field by a computed key, on a model with a renamed field is refused with hook-name-not-compilable.
  • A type-wide hook name means one field in every model. autoPopulatedFields and timestamps apply to every model of the type, so when only some models rename a field, name it there by its stored name (due). A name or expression that would mean different fields in different models is refused with hook-name-not-compilable.
  • An upsert names a constraint first. upsertOn and a batch upsert's constraint address the unique constraint of that name before a unique field, so a constraint keeps working when a renamed field takes the same name.
  • Current names can shorten pages. A read with names=current keeps its answer within the response limit, so a page whose answer in current names would pass the limit holds fewer records. Follow nextCursor.
  • A key spelled like a current name doesn't replace the field. A record written with the new name before the rename reached its database holds that name as an undeclared key beside the stored field. A names=current answer shows the stored field's value under the current name; the undeclared key appears only in the default stored-name answer.
  • A device takes two names for a field. Generated models, and Swift's client.db3.records, accept a field's current and stored names; an older former name is an undeclared field there. Name it by your build's current name in app code.
  • Mapping needs the type's name in the build. client.db3.records maps a model only when its declaration names the type: a generated model, or a schemaToml whose file has [type] name. A model defined with defineModelSchema answers stored names there.
  • A rename reaches each database with the push. Until the push has committed on a database, a write naming the new name there stores it as an undeclared field; follow the push with primitive db3-types push-status workspace.

Changing the type of a field ​

A field's type can't change once a database of the type exists. Replace the field instead, in four pushes. To store size as a number rather than a string:

1. Add the new field beside the old one, and ship app code that writes both:

toml
[models.tasks.fields.size]
type = "string"

[models.tasks.fields.sizeN]
type = "number"

2. Copy each record's value with a server function, called once for each database of the type:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireRole } from "primitive-functions";

// functions/copy-size.ts — copy each task's `size` (a string) into `sizeN`
// (a number). Run it for each database of the type, and again before you clear
// `size`: until then `size` is the source, so a run also updates `sizeN` where
// an older build changed only `size` since the last run.
export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id"],
  authorize: requireRole("admin"),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string }, ctx) => {
    const tasks = ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "workspace").model("tasks");
    let copied = 0;
    let cursor: string | undefined;
    do {
      const page = await tasks.query({ limit: 100, ...(cursor ? { cursor } : {}) });
      for (const task of page.items) {
        if (typeof task.size !== "string") continue;
        const sizeN = Number(task.size);
        if (!Number.isFinite(sizeN) || task.sizeN === sizeN) continue;
        await tasks.patch(String(task.id), { data: { sizeN } });
        copied += 1;
      }
      cursor = page.nextCursor;
    } while (cursor);
    return { copied };
  },
});

3. Deprecate size (deprecated = true), and ship app code that reads sizeN and still writes both.

4. Clear size (cleared = true). Every read then returns sizeN with the copied values and never size; move size to removedFields when you want the name retired for good (Retiring a field).

Until size is cleared it is the source: each run of the copy also updates sizeN wherever a build from before step 1, which writes only size, changed it since the last run. Call the copy once more just before you clear, since a cleared field's values can no longer be read. A size that an older build writes after that last run is lost with the clear, so clear once no build from before step 1 is still writing, or accept losing those writes.

Removing fields on purpose ​

To push a refused change anyway, turn on allowFieldRemoval for the app, push it, then push the change with --allow-field-removal:

toml
# primitive/dev/app.toml
[app]
name = "My App"
mode = "public"
allowFieldRemoval = true
bash
primitive config push                          # stores the setting
primitive config push --allow-field-removal    # pushes the change and lists each one it let through

The flag works only once the setting is stored, so turning it on and using it take two pushes. The override removes the declaration only: values of a removed field stay in stored records, server reads still return them, and a build that still declares the field keeps reading them. To hide a field's values, retire it instead. Each database still judges the revision as above. The setting is the app's own: another app's setting never lets a change through. A type with allowLocalOnly = true refuses removals with the flag too. Delete the line from app.toml and push to turn it off.

Archiving a type ​

Archive a type to stop new databases of it while the ones that exist keep working. Set archived = true in its [type] table and push:

toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/workspace.toml
[type]
name = "workspace"
archived = true

Or let the CLI edit the file and push it for you:

bash
primitive db3-types archive workspace
primitive db3-types unarchive workspace

unarchive removes the line and pushes, and the type takes new databases again. Both commands refuse a type with no local file (run primitive config pull first) and a file with other unpushed changes. primitive db3-types list and get show each type's status. Like any type push, archiving reinstalls the type in each of its databases.

On an archived typeResult
client.db3.create with the typeRefused DB3_TYPE_ARCHIVED
getOrCreateWithAlias when the alias names nothingRefused DB3_TYPE_ARCHIVED
setType on an untyped databaseRefused DB3_TYPE_ARCHIVED
getOrCreateWithAlias when the alias names a database of itAnswers that database
Opening, reading, writing, sharing and deleting its databasesAs before
Pushing a new revision of itAs before; it stays archived

The refusal applies to every caller, admins and functions included. A create made on the device resolves at once, like any create, and the refusal then arrives as db3:create-failed; the records written to it stay on the device:

ts
client.on("db3:create-failed", ({ code, type }) => {
  if (code === "DB3_TYPE_ARCHIVED" && type) ui.showTypeRetired(type);
});

const db = await client.db3.create({ title: "Q3 plan", type: "project" });
swift
// Listen before creating. Hold the subscription for as long as the handler
// should run; dropping it stops the handler.
let failures = client.observeOnMainActor(Db3CreateFailedEvent.self) { [weak ui] failed in
  if failed.code == JsBaoErrorCode.db3TypeArchived.rawValue, let type = failed.type {
    ui?.showTypeRetired(type)
  }
}

// Resolves at once; a refusal arrives later through `failures`.
let db = try await client.db3.create(title: "Q3 plan", type: "project")

Who can create databases of a type ​

By default every member of the app can create a database of any type. To keep a type to app admins and owners, set create = "admins" in its [type] table and push:

toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/team.toml
[type]
name = "team"
create = "admins"

To keep databases with no type to admins and owners too, set untypedDb3Create in app.toml:

toml
# primitive/dev/app.toml
[app]
untypedDb3Create = "admins"

A member's create is then refused with DB3_CREATE_ROLE_REQUIRED (403), and nothing is created:

SettingRefused for a member
create = "admins" on a typeclient.db3.create with the type; getOrCreateWithAlias with the type when the alias names nothing; setType naming the type
untypedDb3Create = "admins"client.db3.create with no type; getOrCreateWithAlias with no type when the alias names nothing

App admins and owners create as before, and so do server functions: a function a member calls can create a restricted database for them with ctx.api.db3.create. Local-only databases (localOnly: true) are never refused. An alias that already names a database still answers it, and "members", or no key, opens the type to every member again.

A create made on the device resolves at once, like any create, and the refusal arrives as db3:create-failed with the database's id, the code and the type (null for a database with no type); the records written to it stay on the device. Offer the create only to users who can make it:

ts
client.on("db3:create-failed", ({ code, type }) => {
  if (code === "DB3_CREATE_ROLE_REQUIRED") ui.showAdminsOnly(type);
});

const db = await client.db3.create({ title: "Design team", type: "team" });
swift
// Listen before creating. Hold the subscription for as long as the handler
// should run; dropping it stops the handler.
let failures = client.observeOnMainActor(Db3CreateFailedEvent.self) { [weak ui] failed in
  if failed.code == JsBaoErrorCode.db3CreateRoleRequired.rawValue {
    ui?.showAdminsOnly(failed.type)
  }
}

// Returns at once; a refusal arrives later through `failures`.
let db = try await client.db3.create(title: "Design team", type: "team")

primitive db3-types list and get show each type's setting.

primitive init sets untypedDb3Create = "admins" on an app it creates for the web template, whose code creates only typed databases; the next config pull writes the line into app.toml. Remove the line and push to let members create untyped databases.

Types for local-only databases ​

To let a type describe local-only databases as well as synced ones, set allowLocalOnly = true in its [type] table and push:

toml
# primitive/dev/db3-types/notes.toml
[type]
name = "notes"
allowLocalOnly = true

The generated code then carries the type's declarations, and a device checks a local-only database of the type against them: its fields, enums, unique keys and indexes. primitive db3-types list and get show the setting, and config pull writes the line.

The server never sees those copies, so it can't tell whether one holds data a change would break. From the push after the one that sets the key, every change must only add:

On a type with allowLocalOnly = trueResult
Adding models, fields, enum values, indexed, unique, constraints, an enum or enforce_enum = true; clearing a field, moving it to removedFields or renaming it; description, class_name or deprecated editsPushes
Any change in the list above under Changing a typeRefused, whether or not a database of the type exists, and with --allow-field-removal too
Un-clearing a field; removing indexed or unique, or removing or changing a constraint, over a field that isn't cleared; adding, changing or removing an existing field's default; removing an enum or enforce_enum; changing any other option of a fieldRefused
Adding a trigger, autoPopulatedFields or timestampsRefused, and a type that has one can't set the key. Put hooks on a second type.
Removing allowLocalOnly, or setting it to falseRefused
Deleting the type: removing its file and pushing with --prune, or DELETE db3-types/<type>, force includedRefused, whether or not a database of the type exists. Keep the file; to stop using the type, stop creating databases of it.
Moving a renamed field to removedFields under its current nameRefused: name its stored name (removedFields = ["due"] for a field with storedAs = "due"), so the generated code hides the same field the server does

Each refusal is DB3_TYPE_NOT_APPEND_ONLY, lists every change with its reason, and has details.allowLocalOnly: true. A new field may carry a default.

Rules the database enforces ​

A type can carry rules the database runs on every create and update, from any writer. They live in the [type] table and in [triggers.<model>]. A bulk load is the exception: it runs none of them.

timestamps stamps create and update times, as epoch milliseconds, into number fields you name:

toml
[type]
name = "workspace"
timestamps = { create = "createdAt", update = "updatedAt" }

Every model is stamped. To stamp only some, list them: timestamps = { create = "createdAt", models = ["tasks"] }. The other models carry no timestamps.

autoPopulatedFields fills fields from the writer. A plain value fills on create; a table names the lifecycles with on:

toml
[type]
name = "workspace"
autoPopulatedFields = { ownerId = "user.userId", editedBy = { value = "user.userId", on = ["update"] } }

It fills only a field that is absent or null in the write.

Triggers compute fields from the record, or refuse a write that breaks a rule:

toml
[triggers.tasks]
triggers = [
  { on = "save", when = "record.status == 'done' && !has(record.completedAt)", set = { completedAt = "now()" } },
  { on = "update", when = "has(record.lockedAt)", refuse = { code = "TASK_LOCKED", message = "This task is locked." } },
]

on is create, update or save (both). when is an optional CEL condition; set maps fields to CEL values, and refuse rejects the write with your code, which the writer receives as DB3_TRIGGER_REFUSED. Expressions see user.userId (the writer), user.writer (the kind of writer), record.* (the record as it will be stored), database.id, now() and lookup(). A rule can never write id.

Reading a field the record doesn't have is an error, not false, so guard optional fields with has():

toml
[triggers.tasks]
triggers = [
  { on = "save", when = "has(record.status) && record.status == 'blocked'", refuse = { code = "TASK_BLOCKED" } },
]

A refusing trigger whose when can't be evaluated refuses the write, with TRIGGER_EVALUATION_FAILED in place of your code; a set trigger whose when can't be evaluated is skipped. has() takes a field path that starts at a name, such as record.status. To test a field of a looked-up record, write lookup('institution', record.id).?syncStartedAt.hasValue(). Push refuses an expression that can never be evaluated, naming the trigger and the failing term.

user.writer tells a member's own write from your app's. Inside a server function user.userId is still the member who invoked it, so a model only your functions should write refuses by the kind of writer instead:

toml
[triggers.ledger]
triggers = [
  { on = "save", when = "user.writer == 'user'", refuse = { code = "LEDGER_PIPELINE_ONLY" } },
]

user.writer is "user" for a member's device or API call, "function" for a server function someone invoked (including functions it starts), and "system" for a run with no caller: a cron fire, a webhook delivery, a database change, or a --as system run. A function acting as a member with asUser writes as "user", so the rule above refuses it too.

The rule stops saves and batches, not a bulk load: anyone who may write the database can still load rows into ledger. It guards against your app's own mistakes, not against a member. For a model members must not write at all, keep it in a sync-off database that only your functions write.

Values a rule set come back to the writer with the write's result, and reach every synced device with the record.

What a record holds ​

A field holds a string, a number, a boolean, null, or a set of strings. Nested objects and arrays of anything but strings aren't stored: flatten them into fields, or type a string field by an object or list def as a JSON field.

  • A field stays one kind. The first non-null value written to a field of a model decides whether it is a string set or a scalar; writing the other kind afterwards is refused with DOCUMENT_ENTRY_INVALID.
  • A model takes at most 1,000 field names. Every name ever written counts, and deleting records frees none.
  • Writing null to a string set empties it.

Reserved field names ​

A field cannot be named type, start with _, or take a name a generated model already uses on either client; writes and type pushes refuse it with RESERVED_FIELD_NAME. Use kind, category or status instead. id is allowed.

The names a generated model uses: CodingKeys, UniqueConstraint, UniqueField, applyAutoStampsForSave, applyStringSetChangeToYMap, clearLocalChanges, constructor, delete, deleteRecordLog, discardChanges, ensureLocalChanges, getChangedFields, getCurrentJSState, getCurrentValue, getDocumentId, getFromYjs, getOrCreateStringSet, getOriginalValue, getStringSetCurrentValues, getStringSetFromYjs, getValue, hasFieldChanged, hasLocalChange, hasUnsavedChanges, hashValue, isDirty, markAllChanged, markStringSetChange, normalizeNonStringSetValue, primitiveValues, related, resolveUnresolvedFormat2Document, save, saveRecordLog, schemaDefaultFor, setValue, syncState, toJSON, validateBeforeSave, validateFieldValue.

A database's observed schema ​

Every database records the fields each model has actually been written with, typed or not. primitive db3 schema <db3-id> shows them beside the declaration, and --toml writes them out as a type file — the quickest way to give a type to a database that grew without one:

bash
primitive db3 schema <db3-id> --toml --output primitive/dev/db3-types/imported.toml

Check the result before pushing it: a field written with more than one kind is commented, and no index is exported.
